summary:
The genome copy number in a nanogram of DNA depends only on the genome size. It returns genome copies, copies per µL in 50 µL, log₁₀ copies and mass of one genome, and the panel shows all of them at once.

The answer depends only on genome size, and it is the number that sets qPCR standard curves, sequencing input and the limit of detection. This calculator converts mass to copies for any genome size. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Genome Copy Number
sections.html:
Copies = mass (g) ÷ (genome length × 660 g/mol) × 6.022 × 10²³

sections.title: How do I use the Genome Copy Number?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: dna mass of 10 ng, genome size of 3.2 Mb.

Substituting them into the formula gives genome copies of 2,851,391, copies per µl in 50 µl of 57,027.82 copies/µL, log₁₀ copies of 6.46, mass of one genome of 3.51 fg.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A human diploid genome weighs about 6.6 pg; a haploid one 3.3 pg. That is the number to remember: one cell, one copy.

  • For qPCR standards, diluting to 10⁶ copies per µL and then serially tenfold gives a clean seven-point curve.

  • Long-read sequencing needs far more mass per copy because the molecules are not amplified — the copy number, not the mass, is what the flow cell sees.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Using genome size in base pairs where the formula expects megabases.
  • Forgetting that a diploid cell contains two copies per genome equivalent.
  • Treating mitochondrial or plasmid DNA with the nuclear genome size.

faq.q: How many copies of a genome are in 1 ng of human DNA?
faq.a: About 303 copies of the 3.2 Gb genome.

faq.q: What is the mass of one copy of the E. coli genome?
What does the Genome Copy Number actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns genome copies, copies per µL in 50 µL, log₁₀ copies and mass of one genome. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
